{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01JXmw9RwRybNfHS5vSpbKJT","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# BUILD PLAN — output format\n2\t\n3\tEmit the plan in exactly these sections, in this order. Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. Phases (Phase 1 onward; dependency order; within a phase, rework widest first, exposure smallest first)\n77\tFor each phase:\n78\t- **Phase N — <name>**\n79\t  - Unlocks: what becomes possible after it.\n80\t  - Depends on: earlier phases and V-IDs, by reference.\n81\t  - Tasks: in order.\n82\t  - Rollback: how this phase is undone, or its point of no return and the gate that guards it.\n83\t  - Exit check: its gates pass, plus any observable condition that no gate covers.\n84\t\n85\t## 6. AI layer (AI/agentic systems only)\n105\t\n106\t| Sublayer | In this system | Built in | Exit check or V-ID |\n107\t|---|---|---|---|\n108\t| 1. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_017LmuZDEuPz1kobVWn9xYt1","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A local command-line tool. It reads each photo's EXIF capture date, plans a new name such as `2024-07-14_153012.jpg`, shows the plan, and then renames the files with an undo log.\n- **Type:** Software (CLI you don't operate); greenfield; small build (one developer, no outside service, no money, no regulated data). It does touch irreplaceable personal files.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness, meaning no photo is ever lost or overwritten.\n- **Worst failure:** A name collision or a crash in the middle of a run overwrites a photo, or leaves the folder half-renamed with no way back.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Data safety | 0 files lost, overwritten or changed in content; undo restores the exact original names | ASSUMPTION (these are irreplaceable personal photos, so any loss is unacceptable) | V2 |\n| Throughput | Dry run of 10,000 JPEGs on a local SSD in under 60 s | ASSUMPTION (the tool reads only file headers; a typical import folder has 1k–10k files) | V0 records the baseline; Phase 2 exit check |\n| Resource use | Peak memory under 200 MB, not growing with folder size | ASSUMPTION (header-only reads; the plan holds only names and dates) | Phase 2 exit check |\n| Operational complexity | One installable package, no services, no network; at most one outside binary (only if V1 switches to exiftool) | ASSUMPTION (one developer) | Phase 2 exit check |\n\n**Missing inputs** (the first one decides whether to build at all):\n1. **Reusable tool or one-off?** If you only need this once, don't build anything. exiftool already does it: `exiftool -d '%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S%%-c.%%e' '-TestName<DateTimeOriginal' DIR` previews the renames, and replacing `TestName` with `FileName` applies them. *My assumption:* you want a tool you'll reuse on every import. Its value over exiftool is safety: preview by default, collisions refused, crash-safe undo.\n2. **File formats and devices** (iPhone HEIC, RAW formats, videos?). This shapes the V1 test set and maybe the EXIF library choice. You supply it before Phase 1.\n3. **Operating systems to support.** This decides how the safe rename is done on each OS and which systems CI tests on. You supply it before Phase 1.\n4. **Naming format.** You confirm it from the Phase 0 preview output.\n5. **Is the folder managed by Lightroom or Apple Photos, or does it have sidecar files** (.xmp, .aae)? Renaming outside a catalog breaks its file references. *My assumption:* plain folders. The tool will refuse to run inside a `.photoslibrary` bundle.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Undo-log format and \"already renamed\" detection | Naming format confirmed on Phase 0 preview output | decision | specified |\n| EXIF library choice and date rules | V1 | validation | specified |\n| Renaming (`--apply`) on any real folder | V2 | risk/security | exposed |\n| V1 test set | Sample files from your actual devices (missing input 2) | organizational | V1 passing (request in Phase 0) |\n| OS-specific rename code and CI test systems | Supported OS list (missing input 3) | organizational | specified |\n| Phase 0 release, then the 1.0 release | TestPyPI/PyPI project name and automated publishing set up | organizational | deployed (Phase 0) / exposed (Phase 2) |\n\nThere are no economic dependencies (no paid services). The only runtime dependency is Python 3.11+, plus exiftool if V1 fails.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| How writes are made safe | R3 (gated for harm: one overwritten photo can't be recovered) | Rename in place in two steps: plan everything first, then execute. Each step is written to an undo log and flushed to disk *before* the rename. Renames never overwrite. Name swaps and loops go through a temporary name. Collisions are checked case-insensitively. | A rename that refuses to overwrite is available on each target OS | V2 | V2 fails on an OS or file system → in-place renaming is disabled there and `--copy-to DIR` is the only way to write |\n| EXIF library | R2 (changes the install story: pure Python vs needing exiftool installed) | Pure-Python `exifread` behind a `DateReader` interface | It reads capture dates correctly for every format you use | V1 | V1 fails for a format you need → switch to PyExifTool; exiftool on PATH becomes a documented prerequisite |\n| Which date, and time-zone handling | R2 (wrong dates get baked into names across a whole library; the undo log limits the damage) | Use `DateTimeOriginal`, falling back to `DateTimeDigitized`. Keep the camera's local time as recorded, with no time-zone conversion. Files with no date are skipped and reported. **No silent fallback to the file's modified time**, which is often the copy date. | Your cameras write `DateTimeOriginal` | V1 | V1 shows a device that only writes another tag → add that tag to the fallback list |\n| Naming format | R2 (once libraries are renamed, a change means renaming them again and breaks \"already renamed\" detection) | `YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS[_NN].<original ext>`. `_NN` numbers photos taken in the same second, ordered by sub-second time and then by original name. | Sortable names with second precision suit you | Your sign-off on the Phase 0 preview | You need another format → add `--format` templates (§10) |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- Build vs buy → build a thin safety layer, unless missing input 1 says one-off, in which case use exiftool.\n- Python 3.11+ installed with `pipx`; `argparse`; `pytest` with `hypothesis`; undo log as JSON Lines.\n- Not recursive by default; extensions keep their original case (changing only the case of a name is risky on case-insensitive file systems).\n\n**N/A:**\n- Monolith vs services, sync vs async, consistency vs availability: it is one local process doing renames in order, and batch consistency is covered by the write-safety row.\n- Data-privacy boundary: nothing ever leaves the machine. \"No network I/O\" is enforced from Phase 0 (§7).\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Real request:** `photo-rename ~/Pictures/2024-import` on a real folder. It responds with an old → new plan table, a summary (to rename / no date / collision / error) and an exit code: 0 = all OK, 1 = some files skipped, 2 = fatal error.\n- **Tiers it crosses:** argument parsing → directory scan (no symlink following) → EXIF read → planner (name + collision check) → output and JSONL log. The executor exists but runs **only in CI against a temporary copy**.\n- **Deploy, log, monitor, roll back:**\n  - Pushing a tag makes CI build the wheel and publish `0.1.0` to TestPyPI.
